chapters.name: Commission, Bond, and Oath
chapters.summary: Who may become a notary, the required course and exam, the 4-year commission, the $15,000 bond, and filing the oath and bond.
keyPoints: Applicants must be at least 18, be California residents, take an approved 6-hour course, and pass the exam.
A commission lasts 4 years, and a notary may act anywhere in California.
The notary must file a $15,000 surety bond and an oath with the county clerk within 30 days after the commission begins.
The bond protects the public; the notary is still personally liable for all damages caused.

chapters.name: Seal, Address Changes, and Commission Records
chapters.summary: What the official seal must look like and contain, how to keep it, and how to report address and name changes.
keyPoints: A round seal may be up to 2 inches across; a rectangular seal up to 1 inch by 2.5 inches.
The seal must show the notary's name, the State Seal, "Notary Public," the county, and the commission expiration date, among other items.
The seal belongs to the notary and must be kept locked; it is destroyed or defaced when the commission ends.
Address changes must be reported to the Secretary of State within 30 days.

chapters.name: Acknowledgments and Jurats
chapters.summary: The two most common notarial acts, what each requires, and how the certificates are completed.
keyPoints: For an acknowledgment, the signer appears in person and declares that they signed; they need not sign in front of the notary.
For a jurat, the signer signs in front of the notary and takes an oath or affirmation.
Both certificates start with a boxed notice saying the notary verifies identity only.
The certificate must be completed at the time the notary signs and seals it.

chapters.name: The Notary Journal
chapters.summary: Keeping one sequential journal, what each entry must contain, the thumbprint rule, and what to do when the journal is lost or requested.
keyPoints: Keep one active sequential journal at a time, in a locked and secured area under your exclusive control.
Each entry includes the date, time, type of act, document type, signer's signature, how identity was proven, and the fee charged.
A right thumbprint is required for deeds, quitclaim deeds, deeds of trust, other real property documents, and powers of attorney.
Report a lost or stolen journal to the Secretary of State immediately.

chapters.name: Certified Copies, Oaths, and Other Acts
chapters.summary: Certified copies a notary may and may not make, oaths and affirmations, signature by mark, and other notary powers.
keyPoints: A notary may certify a copy of a power of attorney, and of a journal entry when the Secretary of State or a court asks.
A notary may not certify copies of birth, death, or marriage records.
An affirmation is a solemn promise on personal honor with no reference to God.
A person who cannot write may sign by mark with witnesses.

chapters.name: Satisfactory Evidence of Identity
chapters.summary: The ID cards a notary may rely on, the five-year rule, and how credible witnesses can identify a signer.
keyPoints: California notaries may not identify a signer by personal knowledge alone.
ID cards must be current or issued within the last five years.
One credible witness who personally knows the notary, or two who do not, may identify a signer who has no ID.
A credible witness must have no financial interest in the document and not be named in it.

chapters.name: Subscribing Witness Notarizations
chapters.summary: How a subscribing witness proves that a principal signed, how the witness is identified, and which documents cannot be proved this way.
keyPoints: A subscribing witness saw the principal sign (or heard the principal acknowledge the signature) and signed as a witness at the principal's request.
The subscribing witness, not the principal, appears before the notary.
The subscribing witness is identified by the oath of a credible witness who shows acceptable ID.
Proofs may not be used for real property documents such as deeds of trust, or for powers of attorney.

chapters.name: Immigration Documents and Foreign Language Advertising
chapters.summary: Limits on notaries who help with immigration matters and the rules for advertising in languages other than English.
keyPoints: A notary who is not an attorney may not give immigration or other legal advice.
Translating "notary public" into Spanish as "notario publico" or "notario" is prohibited.
A non-attorney notary who advertises in another language must post a notice in English and that language saying they are not an attorney.
Violations bring suspension of at least one year or revocation; a second violation means permanent revocation.

chapters.name: Notary Fees
chapters.summary: How the state sets maximum notary fees, when no fee may be charged, and how fees are recorded.
keyPoints: Government Code section 8211 sets maximum fees; a notary may charge less or nothing.
Acknowledgment fees are charged for each signature taken.
No fee may be charged for vote-by-mail ballot materials or veterans' benefit claims.
The fee charged is recorded in the journal; charging more than the law allows is misconduct.

chapters.name: Misconduct, Penalties, and Disqualifying Interest
chapters.summary: Grounds for losing a commission, civil and criminal penalties, and when a notary is disqualified by a personal interest.
keyPoints: The Secretary of State may refuse, suspend, or revoke a commission for grounds such as dishonesty or overcharging.
Civil penalties reach $750 for negligent and $1,500 for willful failures of duty.
Failing to take a required thumbprint can bring a civil penalty of up to $2,500.
A notary may not notarize a transaction in which they have a direct financial or beneficial interest.
